newsitem.title: LEBANON: Pope gets warm welcome in Lebanon.
newsitem.headline: Pope gets warm welcome in Lebanon.

text.p: Pope John Paul arrived in Lebanon on Saturday to a warm welcome from authorities of the Moslem-majority country and immediately issued a veiled call for the departure of Syrian and Israeli troops.

Church bells rang out and a 21-gun salute boomed as the 76-year-old pontiff landed at Beirut airport and stooped as if to kiss a box of Lebanese soil offered by two children after slowly walking down the steps of his plane.
The pope will spend 32 hours in Lebanon on the first visit to the Middle East by a Roman Catholic pontiff since 1964.

Hundreds of civil dignitaries and Moslem and Christian clerics greeted the pope on the tarmac. He walked arm-in-arm with President Elias Hrawi, a pro-Syrian Maronite Christian, to deliver an address from a dais.
Lebanese army troops with binoculars scanned the airport from roofs as others with automatic rifles guarded the area and army helicopters flew overhead.
Hrawi welcomed the pope as "the image of hope for all the Lebanese people" and said Lebanon was trying to consolidate a system defending freedom of belief and dignity for all its people.
The pope, launching immediately into the main themes of his visit, said Lebanon was a country seeking independence and freedom whose national territory should be recognised and respected by all.

This appeared to be a reference to the presence of 35,000 Syrian troops stationed in Lebanon and of some 2,000 Israeli troops who hold a south Lebanon border strip comprising some 12 percent of the country.

"It is as a friend of Lebanon that I come to encourage the sons and daughters of this land of hospitality, this country of ancient spiritual and cultural traditions, so desirous of independence and freedom," the pope said.

All Lebanese citizens should be allowed a place in the country's political and economic life, he added in an indirect reference to complaints by some members of the country's Christian minority that they are marginalised from politics.

John Paul said throughout his pontificate he had frequently alerted the international community "to help the Lebanese people to once again find peace in a national territory recognised and respected by all."
All Lebanese should be committed to peace and reconciliation, the pope said.

"In this new Lebanon which you are slowly rebuilding it is important to give a place to every citizen, particularly to those who, inspired by legitimate patriotism, wish to become involved in political activity or economic life," he added.
"From this point of view, the first condition for any truly democratic process is a just balance between the vital forces of the nation..."
Flag-waving crowds lined Christian areas along the 10-km (six miles) long route as the pope drove in his Popemobile to the presidential palace in the hills above Beirut.
The route was decorated with a forest of papal and Lebanese flags and lined with troops carrying automatic rifles every few metres (yards).

The crowds appeared in a festive mood in Christian districts, but the welcome was sparse along the road through Moslem areas where few people were on the streets and many appeared to have taken the day off to go to the beach.
The pope was due to have talks with Hrawi and other officials at the palace including billionaire Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri, a Sunni Moslem. He will also meet Moslem spiritual leaders.
He will later fly by helicopter to the Christian heartland north of Beirut for an evening meeting with thousands young people.
